meaning: Showing no thought or feeling; also empty, not occupied
trick: VACANT = VACATION in the mind: nobody home.
examples: She was distracted and vacant most of the time, except when he called her name.
He gave me a vacant stare when I asked the question.

meaning: Showing no intelligence or serious thought
trick: VACUOUS = like a VACUUM: empty inside.
examples: He saw Japan as a vacuous nation full of hippies.
The movie was fun but vacuous.

meaning: Not clear, exact or detailed
trick: VAGUE sounds like a WAVE - blurry, moving, unclear.
examples: Rumours of a wonderful farm kept spreading in vague and distorted forms.
He gave only a vague answer about his plans.

usage.pattern: vague about something / a vague + noun

meaning: In a slight or unclear way
trick: VAGUE + LY: in a not-quite-clear way.
examples: Oblong and glossy, it vaguely reminded me of the pen trays in the office.
I vaguely remember meeting her years ago.

meaning: Too proud of your looks or abilities; also useless or unsuccessful
trick: VAIN people look in the mirror again and again; VAIN effort goes down the drain.
examples: Women are shallow and vain and will never like me!
She is so vain that she checks her phone camera all day.

meaning: In a brave and determined way
trick: VALIANT = VALOUR: brave knight fights VALIANTLY.
examples: She said he fought valiantly.
The team tried valiantly but lost the match.

meaning: Great bravery, especially in battle; US spelling (British valour)
trick: VALOR = VALue of a brave heart.
examples: He won a Silver Star and four Bronze Stars for valor.
The soldier received a medal for valor.

meaning: Small flaps in the heart (or a pipe) that open and close to control flow
trick: VALVES let blood flow one way, like a one-way door.
examples: He talked nonstop while he checked out all my chambers and valves.
The doctor said his heart valves are healthy.

usage.pattern: heart valves / the valves of something

meaning: Too much pride in your looks or abilities
trick: VANITY - VAIN-ity: a VAIN person's quality.
examples: We had thought that Snowball's rebellion was caused simply by his vanity and ambition.
She bought the costly bag out of vanity.

meaning: A place or position from which you can see or understand things well (usually followed by 'point')
trick: VANTAGE = adVANTAGE spot to see from.
examples: From my vantage point I could see the crest of the hill above.
From this vantage point, you can see the whole city.

meaning: To disappear completely; also to turn into gas
trick: VAPOR-IZE: turn into VAPOR and vanish.
examples: If a beginner died, his race would vaporize overnight.
The water will vaporize if you heat it.

meaning: Amounts by which things differ or change
trick: VARIANCES = how much things VARY.
examples: I studied the course and noted temperature and elevation variances.
The teacher noticed small variances in the test scores.

meaning: Changed or been different (past of vary); also of many different types
trick: VARIED = VARY + ED: never the same.
examples: For eight years that walk has never varied.
Her lunch varied from day to day.

usage.pattern: something has varied / a varied + noun

meaning: Covered with a clear shiny liquid that dries hard
trick: VARNISHED: a VARNISH coat makes wood shine.
examples: Oblong, glossy, varnished black all over, it reminded me of the pen trays.
The varnished table shone in the light.

meaning: US: the main sports team of a school or college; also British informal for university
trick: VARSITY = uniVERSITY's best team.
examples: It was no surprise when he made the varsity squad.
She plays on the varsity basketball team.

meaning: Decorative containers for holding flowers
trick: VASES hold flowers; say 'vaa-zes'.
examples: She saw the marble bases of statues and the lower halves of vases.
She put fresh roses in both vases.

meaning: A person or country that owes loyalty and service to a more powerful one
trick: VASSAL serves the CASTLE lord.
examples: The Romans forced the princes of vassal states to send their sons to Rome.
The small kingdom became a vassal of the empire.

usage.pattern: a vassal of someone / vassal state

meaning: Extremely large in size or amount
trick: VAST = Very And Superbly Tall/big.
examples: She would admire Jalil for his vast and worldly knowledge.
The desert is a vast area of sand.

usage.pattern: a vast + noun / the vast majority

meaning: Having an arched roof or ceiling
trick: VAULTED roof jumps in an arch, like a pole VAULT.
examples: They would take walks together in the vaulted bazaar.
The old church has a high vaulted ceiling.

meaning: Changed direction suddenly
trick: VEERED: the car VEERED like a deer jumping sideways.
examples: As he veered onto the highway and headed home, he kept on ranting.
The bike veered to avoid the dog.

meaning: Moving or changing direction towards something
trick: VEERING = steering away in a new direction.
examples: My splintering marriage was veering toward divorce.
The talk kept veering away from the main topic.

meaning: Plants in general, especially in a particular area
trick: VEGETATION = all the VEGETABLES and plants growing.
examples: The path is rough and dim beneath the vegetation and undergrowth.
The hills are covered with thick vegetation.

meaning: Informal: vegetables
trick: VEGGIES = VEGetables, cute short form.
examples: The ticket to good health comes from eating your veggies.
Kids should eat more veggies.

meaning: Strong and forceful feeling, especially in speaking
trick: VEHEMENCE: speaking with the force of a VEHICLE crashing in.
examples: 'In short,' he concluded, speaking with great vehemence, 'I accuse the prisoner.'
She denied the rumour with vehemence.

usage.pattern: with vehemence / the vehemence of something

meaning: A piece of thin cloth worn to cover the face or head; also something that hides
trick: VEIL hides the face - it VEILS (covers) like a curtain.
examples: Through the veil, Mariam saw a tall man stooping in the doorway.
The bride wore a long white veil.

usage.pattern: wear a veil / through a veil / a veil of something

meaning: Covered with a veil; also hidden or not openly said
trick: VEIL + ED = put a VEIL on it.
examples: She imagined her smiling shyly behind a veiled green gown.
He made a veiled threat during the meeting.

meaning: A particular style or way of speaking or writing; also a tube carrying blood to the heart
trick: Talking in the same VEIN - like blood flowing on the same path.
examples: I was going on in the same vein, when he cut in with a question.
The next speech continued in a similar vein.

usage.pattern: in the same vein / in a similar vein

meaning: Soft and smooth like velvet
trick: VELVETY = feels like VELVET.
examples: I stared into the velvety, jade mountains.
The cat has velvety fur.

meaning: A long, bitter fight in which people keep taking revenge
trick: VENDETTA = VENGEANCE + DEBT: a debt of revenge.
examples: He was caught up in some sordid vendetta in the city's underworld.
The two families carried on a vendetta for years.

meaning: An outward look that hides the real feelings; also a thin layer of wood on furniture
trick: VENEER = a thin layer that just APPEARS nice on the outside.
examples: I kept all my weaknesses locked down beneath an iron veneer.
Behind his veneer of calm, he was nervous.

usage.pattern: a veneer of something / beneath a veneer

meaning: Harm done to someone in return for harm they did
trick: VENGEANCE sounds like 'vengeance = revenge-ance'.
examples: There was not an animal on the farm that did not take vengeance on them.
The hero swore vengeance on the villain.

usage.pattern: take vengeance on someone / with a vengeance

meaning: To express or release a strong feeling or energy
trick: VENT: a pressure VENT lets the steam out.
examples: On easy runs I felt a surge of adrenaline that I couldn't vent.
Go for a run to vent your anger.

meaning: Expressed or released a strong feeling, often on someone
trick: VENTED: let off steam like a pressure cooker VENT.
examples: She went straight to frustration and vented it by yelling at me.
He vented his anger on his younger brother.

meaning: Expressing strong feelings, especially anger or worry, to feel better
trick: VENTING = letting out the steam through a VENT.
examples: What started as a spontaneous venting session had become a solo intervention.
After a bad day, she spent an hour venting to her friend.

usage.pattern: venting to someone / a venting session

meaning: To go somewhere unknown or risky; also a new business project
trick: adVENTURE - VENTURE out on an adventure.
examples: Let us accompany the young man and venture beyond the door.
It was too cold to venture outside.

usage.pattern: venture out/into somewhere / a business venture

meaning: Green with lots of grass and plants
trick: VERDANT: VERD = green (like VERDE in Spanish).
examples: Shiva was walking in the verdant gardens of the royal guest house.
Cows grazed on the verdant hills.

meaning: A final decision or opinion, often of a court
trick: VERDICT: VERI (true) + DICT (said) = what's declared true.
examples: Long before the box-office verdict on the films was clear, readers gave the book a thumbs-up.
The jury will give its verdict tomorrow.

usage.pattern: the verdict on something / reach a verdict

meaning: Came very close to a certain state
trick: VERGED: stood on the VERGE (edge) of it.
examples: Any activity would spike my heart rate until I verged on collapse.
Her excitement verged on panic.

meaning: Coming very close to a certain state
trick: VERGING = at the VERGE (edge) of something.
examples: I could feel it verging on hot-air-balloon status.
His confidence was verging on arrogance.

meaning: Used to stress that something is really like what you say
trick: VERITABLE: VERI = true (like VERIfy).
examples: There were veritable epidemics of fear going on in the media.
Her garden is a veritable jungle.

meaning: Small animals or insects that are harmful, like rats and cockroaches
trick: VERMIN = VERY MEAN pests.
examples: I had to figure out how to clear the restaurant of vermin.
The old barn was full of vermin.

usage.pattern: clear something of vermin / infested with vermin

meaning: A short numbered part of a holy book; also poetry, or a part of a song
trick: VERSE: one line in the UNIVERSE of a holy book.
examples: She remembered a verse from the Koran that Mullah Faizullah had taught her.
The children learned a verse from the poem.

meaning: Compared with; also against (in a game or case)
trick: VERSUS = VS on a match poster.
examples: It helps show us what's good for us versus what's bad for us.
It's India versus Australia tonight.

usage.pattern: something versus something / someone versus someone

meaning: A feeling that everything is spinning, often when looking down from high up
trick: VERTIGO: VERTICAL drop makes your head GO round.
examples: Standing close to the edge of a cliff brings on a heady sense of vertigo.
She gets vertigo on tall buildings.

usage.pattern: suffer from vertigo / a sense of vertigo

meaning: Used to stress the exact person, place or thing; also extremely
trick: 'This VERY spot' = this EXACT spot.
examples: I'll meet you at this very spot.
He left on that very day.

meaning: A sleeveless jacket, such as a life jacket; also (British) an undershirt
trick: VEST covers your chest, no sleeves.
examples: Strapped into a buoyancy vest with a wounded knee, I could hardly swim.
Wear a life vest on the boat.

meaning: A person who has served in the armed forces; also someone with long experience
trick: VETERAN = a VET who has seen it all (experience).
examples: Metz was a veteran.
Veteran runners had an 8 a.m. start.

meaning: To annoy or worry someone
trick: VEX sounds like 'wrecks' your mood.
examples: I'd have preferred not to vex him.
Don't vex your mother with silly questions.

meaning: The ability to work, succeed or survive
trick: VIABILITY: VIA = a way it can go = it's workable.
examples: We won't go into the biological viability of sitting in one spot for forty-nine days.
The bank checked the viability of the business plan.

meaning: Able to work or succeed in practice; also able to live or grow
trick: VIABLE = VIA-ABLE: there is a way (via) and you are able.
examples: That something can be the smallest viable action toward something else.
Selling online is a viable option for small shops.

meaning: The area near or around a place or person
trick: VICINITY sounds like 'vicinity = nearby city' – the area close by.
examples: Whenever a kid cried in their vicinity, Aziza was quick to explain it away.
There are three schools in the vicinity of our house.

meaning: Cruel and violent, meant to hurt; also very strong or severe (of pain, weather)
trick: VICIOUS has VICE in it – full of vice, cruel.
examples: Other times she knew she teed herself up for a vicious beat down.
The dog gave a vicious bark at the stranger.

meaning: The state of being, or seeing yourself as, a victim
trick: VICTIM + HOOD (like childhood) = the state of being a victim.
examples: The biggest problem with victimhood chic is that it takes attention away from actual victims.
He refused to live in victimhood after the accident.

usage.pattern: a sense of victimhood / claim victimhood

meaning: Having won a fight, game or struggle
trick: VICTORY + -OUS = full of victory.
examples: Pass on this message so that future generations carry on the struggle until it is victorious.
Our team was victorious in the final match.

meaning: To compete hard with others to get something
trick: VIE sounds like 'war-ee' – you go to war for it, you compete.
examples: We instinctually measure ourselves against others and vie for status.
Two shops vie for customers on the same street.

usage.pattern: vie for something / vie with someone (for something)

meaning: A time of staying awake at night to watch over someone or pray; also a quiet gathering to remember someone
trick: VIGIL is the root of VIGILANT – staying awake and watchful.
examples: I can spend the night there, keeping the usual vigil beside the body.
She kept a vigil by her sick mother's bed.

usage.pattern: keep a vigil (beside/by someone) / hold a vigil

meaning: Carefully watching for danger or problems
trick: VIGILANT = keeping VIGIL, eyes always open.
examples: I remained hyper vigilant, scanning for any physical issues that could crop up.
Stay vigilant when you walk home late at night.

meaning: Times of staying awake to watch, wait or pray
trick: VIGILS = many nights of VIGIL, eyes open, waiting.
examples: She kept her vigils for the Mujahideen and waited for her parade.
The family held vigils outside the hospital every night.

meaning: With a lot of energy and force
trick: VIGOR = energy; VIGOROUSLY = with full energy.
examples: The young fellows were taking longer strides and gesturing more vigorously than usual.
She shook the bottle vigorously before opening it.

meaning: Extremely unpleasant, wicked or disgusting
trick: VILE is EVIL with letters shuffled (V-I-L-E).
examples: Their fear was drowned in their rage against this vile, contemptible act.
The milk had gone bad and smelled vile.

meaning: The feeling or fact of being shown to be right after doubt or blame
trick: VINDICATION – you WIN and are INDICATED as right.
examples: In these dreams, Nana cackled with delight and vindication.
The test result was a vindication of her hard work.

usage.pattern: a vindication of something / feel vindication

meaning: Climbing plants with long stems, especially grape plants
trick: VINES give grapes for WINE.
examples: Grape vines were clinging to wooden trellises in Jalil's garden.
Green vines covered the old wall.

meaning: A kind of strong plastic; also old-style music records made of it
trick: VINYL rhymes with 'final' – the final spin of the record.
examples: She ran her hands over the vinyl, flowered curtains that smelled like burned meals.
My uncle still plays old songs on vinyl.

meaning: Good moral qualities; also advantages or good points of something
trick: VIRTUES sounds like 'vir-true' – true goodness.
examples: I tried to understand the wisdom and virtues of the faith I have lived by.
Patience and honesty are great virtues.

usage.pattern: the virtues of something / extol the virtues of something

meaning: In a way felt deeply in the body or emotions, not just thought
trick: VISCERA = guts; VISCERALLY = felt in the guts.
examples: I felt it viscerally, and I used that idea to start something new.
She reacted viscerally to the sad news.

meaning: The stiff front part of a cap that shades the eyes; also a see-through face cover on a helmet
trick: VISOR protects your VISION from the sun.
examples: The doorman was dressed in a burgundy suit and visor cap.
He pulled down his visor to block the sun.

usage.pattern: a visor cap / pull down the visor

meaning: Extremely important or necessary; also full of life and energy
trick: VITAL = needed for life (vita = life), like vitamins.
examples: I knew it was vital to get in some hundred-mile weeks.
Water is vital for all living things.

usage.pattern: it is vital to do something / vital for/to something

meaning: Lively, bright and full of energy (usually of a person)
trick: VIVA = life; VIVACIOUS = full of life.
examples: Snowball was a more vivacious pig than Napoleon, quicker in speech.
Our new teacher is vivacious and fun.

meaning: Very bright in colour; also very clear and detailed, like real life
trick: VIVID = full of life (viv-), colours that pop.
examples: The hot red soil was dappled with vivid green.
I had a vivid dream last night.

meaning: In a very clear and detailed way
trick: VIVIDLY remember = the picture is still alive in your mind.
examples: I vividly recall one night we were so broke we drove home on an almost empty tank.
I vividly remember my first day at school.

meaning: Schools that teach practical skills for a particular job or trade
trick: VOCATION = job; VOCATIONAL schools train you for a job.
examples: They also send students to vocational schools.
He learned plumbing at one of the vocational schools in town.

meaning: Likely to change suddenly, especially to anger; also (of prices) going up and down quickly
trick: VOLATILE – like a VOLcano, can blow up anytime.
examples: She lived in fear of his shifting moods and his volatile temperament.
Petrol prices have been volatile this year.

meaning: Done because you choose to, not because you are forced
trick: VOLUNTARILY = like a VOLUNTEER, of your own will.
examples: It can be hard to tell doing something out of obligation from doing it voluntarily.
He voluntarily gave up his seat for the old man.

meaning: In a very hungry or eager way; also eagerly wanting a lot of something (e.g. reading)
trick: VORACIOUSLY – sounds like 'war on dishes', eating everything.
examples: The waiter brought the starter, which she wolfed down voraciously.
He reads books voraciously.

meaning: A serious promise to do something
trick: VOW – say 'WOW, I promise!'
examples: He made a vow to himself that they would not spend another winter in camp.
She made a vow to quit sugar.

meaning: Promised seriously to do something
trick: VOWED = made a VOW.
examples: The guitarist had gotten over his self-pity and had vowed to start a new band.
She vowed never to be late again.

usage.pattern: vowed to do something / vowed that ...

meaning: A long journey, especially by sea or into space
trick: VOYAGE sounds like 'boy-age' – a boy's long trip across the sea.
examples: People were starting on a voyage to a world which no longer concerned me.
The ship's voyage took two months.

usage.pattern: go on / start on a voyage (to somewhere)
